Technique Added: For the water bottle I added one technique at a time. V2 added a role at the start ("You are an expert e-commerce copywriter..."). V3 added context like the product details, who the customer is, and that it goes on a Shopify page. V4 added constraints like under 120 words, the tone, words to avoid, and things it had to mention. V5 added an output format with a headline, a short paragraph, and 4 bullets. V6 added a few-shot example of a backpack description at the end. For the backpack I used role, context, constraints, and output format. For the coffee subscription I used role, context, constraints, and a few-shot example of a snack box caption.

Version: How each technique changed the output
Technique Added: The role in V2 mostly changed the tone. It sounded more outdoorsy, but the content was about the same and the headline only added "Refillable." Context in V3 made the biggest jump because it used every spec I gave it, but it also got longer. Constraints in V4 cut it down to one paragraph around 80 words and it still kept all the features. The output format in V5 made it way easier to read. However, the first bullet got vague and the headline didn't say what the product was. The few-shot example in V6 changed the style the most. "Fill Up. Head Out." copied "Pack Light. Go Far." almost exactly. It did drop the plastic waste point though, so that part got a little worse.

Version: When it ignored my prompt or made things up
Technique Added: It didn't really make things up, which surprised me. Even V1 said it had no specs to work with. The backpack added small things like "in low light" that I didn't give it. In V6 it skipped the plastic waste point even though that was in the customer info. For the coffee caption it never used the word "fresh," but it showed it with the 48 hour roast detail. I didn't rerun these, but next time I would add a rule like "mention reducing plastic waste." Also, I had ChatGPT memory turned on for at least the first two versions, so that might have affected the results a little.

Context made the biggest difference. Without details the model can only write something vague, and the role only changed how it sounded. Once it had real specs and a customer, the descriptions actually started sounding like something you'd see on a real store page. Few-shot was second because it changed the style more than any rule did.
